analysis.title: Hotter US inflation leaves the market gunning for rate hikes
key_insights: September core CPI rose 0.3% on the month and 2.6% over the year, slightly hotter than the consensus forecast of 0.2% and 2.5%.
September headline CPI was 0.6% on the month and 3.7% over the year, in line with expectations. A 9.1% monthly jump in gasoline prices drove the headline.
Shelter, the largest component by weight, rose 0.4% on the month after three softer prints that averaged 0.2%.
Airline fares rose 1.2% on the month on higher fuel costs, and the shutdown of Spirit Airlines has removed competition. Used vehicles rose 0.7% and recreation rose 0.5%.
Softer components were food (0.0%), medical care (+0.1%) and education and communication (0.2%).
Monthly core inflation is running well above the 0.17% monthly average ING says is needed to bring annual inflation back to 2% over time.

ING thinks the data is probably not strong enough to make the Fed hike in October, since officials have said they are in no hurry after the 25bp hike in September. Futures now price a 45% chance of an October hike, up from about 20% before the data.

The inflation outlook depends on the Strait of Hormuz. Refined fuel prices are still rising and could feed into a broader range of categories. The tech/AI data centre roll-out is also adding to price pressure. Fed hikes will have limited effect on either driver.

ING expects a cooling housing market to bring softer shelter inflation, and a less onerous tariff regime to help. Wage growth is the key variable, running at about 3% in a low-hire, low-fire labour market, with risk of further slowing that would dampen prices over the medium to longer term.
ING forecasts a December Fed rate hike followed by a long pause. It sees risks skewed toward higher rates before cuts arrive.

tension_points.bull_case: Hotter core inflation and rising fuel prices keep the market pricing more hikes. Futures show a 45% chance of an October hike, and ING's own forecast includes a December hike.
tension_points.bear_case: Wage growth of about 3%, a weak housing market and a lighter tariff regime should slow inflation over time, which gives scope for an eventual reversal.
tension_points.what_invalidates: A further slowdown in wage growth, or softer shelter prints as the housing market cools, would weaken the case for more hikes. Further gains in refined fuel prices tied to the Strait of Hormuz would strengthen it.
